utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we just tidy up a few things arising from yesterday's cross-examination and sort out the exhibits. But before I come to those, there is one point that I would have dealt with in re-examination which I think is important to point out straight away. The Court may remember some cross-examination about the discoveries at Racak by an Irish OSCE member called Eamonn Smith, and there was the suggestion being made that ammunition of Chinese manufacture had been found. And when challenged about the nature of his cross-examination, the accused moved us on. Now, the statement of Smith and another man with whom he was working at the time say absolutely nothing about Chinese manufacture. On the contrary, the only identification so far as the ammunition is concerned in both of their statements taken together is that there was Cyrillic writing on some of the ammunition found in the area. The matter having been raised, I'll deal with it evidentially, probably, in due course, as I now must. The exhibits, we've done our best to make things easy for the -- for us overnight by draft translations of untranslated documents, but I've barely looked at some of them myself because they've only just become available. Can I suggest we -- to avoid things getting unsatisfactory or being found to be unsatisfactory later, can I suggest that we deal with the exhibits that the accused presented in the order in which he presented them. So if we start with Exhibit D2, which is this document, we do have a translation in English of that, and I'm going to invite the Chamber to say that this is not a document that it should accept at the moment because it's basically an expert report. Now, expert reports can be admitted as part of a party's evidence, and if they are presented, the other party has a right to cross-examine. If this document is simply taken, its status is entirely unclear but it no doubt will be relied upon as an expert's report without the expert being called. So if I can ask you to consider it and with that objection in mind. You will see that it's a publication, scientific journal, headed the Racak case, then there are the authors, Dobricanin, Matejic, Milosevic and Jaksic. There is then -- the subject, it's a discussion of the Racak incident and the result of autopsies on the bodies. There's then a history. And then over the page, an introduction and some reference to factual matters, as we can see, with William Walker's name. Then on the third page, the findings and discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We see this. One suggestion is that we mark it for identification and not admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can't improve on that. Then can we come to the next one, which is D3. This one was a document I was going to introduce in re-examination myself in any event, and I did ask the witness one question about it. It's the report of the Judge, the investigating local Judge, Danica Marinkovic, and we have a draft translation for you of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've already referred to the one point that I wanted to refer to, and so there's no objection to that as a document. We then come --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's hand those round so we've got them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next document is D4, which the accused presented without any translation. We do have this in-house so there's no challenge to its provenance or anything of that sort, and I've now been able to provide a draft report -- draft translation. So although we're using the version submitted by the accused, there being no reason not to, it does exist in the files here with the ERN number should we need it. The draft translation of D4 shows it to be an on-site investigation report, signed again by that same judge, and summarising bodies found and dealing with the report of lists of weapons, trenches, and so on. So that becomes D4. There are then three more documents, and I don't know what numbers have been associated with which and in which order. He handed in three more documents, which we've tried to process overnight and we have now obtained draft translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are these the Internet documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not sure what he said about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, before we get there, there is the extract from the Human Rights Watch book.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. Well, that book we have for you. We don't have quite enough copies to meet our usual copy provision duties, but we have enough for the Chamber and Registry and the accused and so on. And it's much like "As Seen As Told," the book summarising events from all perspectives, and the accused wanted it to go before you and we would be happy for that to happen. So can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. That should have -- that should have the next number. Which is the number of the book, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we actually skipped one before we get to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Because we've given another Exhibit D5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's go back to the book. That would suit you if it's D6, would it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. D6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So the book will be D6. Now let us go back to D5.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if the Registry could hold up whichever D5 is so that I know which one it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you give it to me, I'll deal with it. Yes. Of course, having said that, it's in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If Your Honour could hold it up, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's the number numbered 4 by the accused. Perhaps the simplest thing is to hand it to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Right. We can hand in a draft translation of that. I have barely read it myself. It's a document that purports to be from the Republic of Serbia's Autonomous Province of Kosovo, dated the 9th of March 1999. It says that it is official notes made on the 9th of March, following the analysis of material from the pre-criminal proceedings in connection with the Racak incident. And the draft and probably summary translation goes on to say that the deaths were not caused by a criminal act committed by members of the RS MUP. Now, I know nothing of this document. I'm in no position to accept its authenticity. I know nothing of its provenance, and I find it hard to see how it can be admitted for any purposes save if it's admitted for -- at this stage for identification but not for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will mark it for identification and not admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, there are two more documents. One appears to be an extract from a book and one is something that the draft translation is apparently part of a speech, although the single sheet -- I don't know which number is going for which at the moment. Can we come to the one-page document next or the, I think it's the three- or four-page document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there a further extract from a book?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. If this is the extract from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've got two now in front of us. One is the excerpt from the book, the other one is a draft speech. Turning first to the excerpt from the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we can be told what number that would have. I'm not going to object to its production. I don't know anything about the book at the moment. The Chamber will see that the points that I think the accused rely on are on the second page of the draft translation where there's a reference to Mrs. Ranta, and the Court's already indicated to the accused that Mrs. Ranta can always be called as a witness if her material is to go in. Whether the book should be identified at this stage as an exhibit or simply produced for identification purposes is a matter about which I'm comparatively neutral.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think this would be 7; is that right? D7?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be marked Defence Exhibit D7.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is that being produced or for identification only?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll consider that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll admit that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. And then the last one, I think, which must become Exhibit 8 is a -- Exhibit 8 is simply a photocopy, as I have it, a part photocopy of part of a sheet of paper which is said in the draft translation to be a draft speech for the second anniversary of the Lodza battle, and it is a speech praising the KLA. Where it comes from, who is it by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll mark that for identification. D8; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In which case, Your Honour, I think that tidies up the exhibits from yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. There are, I'm told, three other documents which the accused wished to have admitted. Perhaps I could have them in front of me. They are marked -- he has marked them 8, 9, and 10. They are, apparently, one from the Wall Street Journal -- in any event, have you got these?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I haven't seen them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it would be convenient -- we will stop there for the moment on these exhibits. You might like to have a look at those ones, and you can address us on it. And I will also explain to the accused what has happened so far and give him the chance to address us on it. Mr. Milosevic, as you've heard, we've been going through the various documents which you produced yesterday and asked for admission. The last three which have come from the Internet we will deal with later when the Prosecution have had a chance of considering them. The position is this: That we've admitted all the documents so far but for two -- three, I should say. We have not admitted the report from the scientific journal of the faculty of medicine. That appears to be an expert report. At the moment, it's been marked for identification, which means that it's been noted that it's been put in but it hasn't been admitted, and you'll have to call evidence about that if you want it admitted. The next item which we've not admitted is described as an official note of the Republic of Serbia, Province of Kosovo and Metohija, District Public Prosecutor's Office, dated the 9th of March, 1999. And similarly, the letter on the second anniversary of the Lodza battle, again a draft. And the reason that they have not been admitted but simply marked for identification is that they -- the provenance where these items come from isn't clear. And again, if you want them admitted, you'll have to call some evidence about that to explain what the documents are. Now, is there anything you want to say to us about that since you haven't had the opportunity of addressing us?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me start from the last one. As for this exhibit, I tendered it when the witness was questioned about the presence of foreign elements within the terrorist organisation of the KLA. It's no draft. It is a telegram that was published. It was sent by one of the KLA commanders to the participants in the anniversary of the Lodza battle. They consider that to be important. You may remember that this was near Pec. Some witnesses here said the civilians had been attacked. It was a major battle with large scale KLA forces involved. In this telegram, he thanks the fighters of the KLA and the foreign units or, rather, participants from other countries, which is, doubtless, additional proof that one of their so-called commanders pays homage to these foreigners. And this is linked to the other exhibits that you are going to look at subsequently that speak of the presence of Al Qaeda in Kosovo and also other terrorist organisations that are very well known in the world. So this corroborates from their side as well - that is to say from the side of the Albanian terrorists - the presence in their own ranks of foreign fighters, these holy fighters of Al Qaeda, et cetera. So I think that it can certainly be admitted into evidence. Number two that you mentioned that you not including, that you are not admitting, that is the public prosecutor who is in charge, and he looked at this according to the law on criminal proceedings in Yugoslavia. He looked at the Racak case, and he established that in accordance with the law on the interior, the police intervened, or, rather, that no crime was committed there. That is the position of the state authority in charge, that is to say the public prosecutor in charge, whose sole right is to establish whether there are grounds for criminal prosecution or not. So this is an official document, and therefore, I believe that it should also be admitted into evidence. As for this Praxis Medica scientific journal which has not been admitted so far either, I bore in mind that this document was marked by a number given by this other side, K021747 -- 0212747, that is, and the other pages, 8, 9, 10. Many facts were presented there, and this denies any possibility of presenting Racak as a crime. This is not a political text, this is a professional text, and it looks at the thoughts expounded by university professors and other persons who were involved in the entire proceedings. So I believe this should be admitted into evidence too. I also would like to say, and I hope that I'm not making a mistake because I'm not familiar with your procedures, this also means that the tapes I played here and that have to do with everything that you have seen - I don't have to describe all of that now, the presence, et, et cetera - that all this should be exhibits too because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me stop you there and see if there's any opposition to that. The tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That the tapes be exhibited? They should be. I had overlooked that and they should have been given a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we should have dealt with it at the time. What would a number be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We will give the videotape Defence Exhibit D9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, since you mentioned your lack of familiarity with the procedures, I'd like to point out that the forensic report that you sought to have tendered is governed by a particular procedure, the testimony of expert witnesses, and what is to be done is that you should file the statement of the forensic analyst as an expert witness, and the other party will have, I think it is 30 days within which to indicate whether it accepts the statement or whether it wishes to cross-examine the expert witness, which is the point that Mr. Nice made. So that the other party does have a right to cross-examine, and that is why we were not able to admit it. If the other party wishes to accept that statement, then the statement can be admitted and would be admitted without cross-examination. So that is the particular procedure relating to the forensic report, and you will no doubt wish to bear that in mind. Well, the other -- the other exhibits that you sought to have tendered, we have marked for identification for different reasons relating to the provenance, as explained by the Presiding Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may assist the accused, now that he's obviously researching the materials we're supplying to him, to understand that where material is supplied under, for example, Rule 68 as being potentially exculpatory, that doesn't mean it can simply go in as an exhibit because it's been produced by us. It's simply handed over by us as material that may assist him, but the rules of production of exhibits are still going to apply. As to the newspaper articles, I'll read them as soon as I can. In any event, the Court will remember that there's an outstanding bundle of newspaper articles that were considered in part by the accused, put in in part by the accused, and being further considered by us. It may be in due course it will be sensible to have a single collection of newspaper articles and simply to add to them with any newspaper articles that the Chamber thinks is useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We should deal with those three before we forget the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll deal with them all collectively, I hope, by tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think, incidentally, it was more than one video that the accused produced. The booth will know. I think it was three or two rather than one in three parts.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was one video and he had different segments on one video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Mr. Nice, while you're on your feet, it may be convenient to deal with another matter, which is the next batch of Rule 92 bis witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be you're not in a position to deal with them, but can I indicate the preliminary view of the Trial Chamber about them? It reflects particularly K5. The witnesses who deal with Racak - that's Bilal, Avdu, Drita Emini, Agron Mehmeti, and Xhemajl Beqiri, Nesret Shabani, those statements are all admissible. However, the Chamber is not at the moment satisfied as to K5.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is the -- can I come back to K5 at a slightly later stage? You mean he's not permissible under 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not sure that's an appropriate procedure, given the nature of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In which case, if that's the provisional view, and unless I'm able to persuade you to the contrary, his evidence will have to be given in full.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The issue of the summarising witness will turn up fairly soon. That's Barney Kelly. I'm going to have prepared, I hope today, a note on the relevant law. It's been before this Chamber similarly but not identically composed in the past and will be familiar territory but it ought to be served on the amici and on the accused and I'll try to have that done today or tomorrow so that a very short oral presentation by me will remind the Chamber of the issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I have a couple of minutes in private session to deal with protection of witnesses, but it really is only a couple of minutes and then we'll be ready to press on with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just before the witness is called by Mr. Saxon, one other administrative matter. The next report on disclosure under Rule 68 will be served on all the parties, I hope, tomorrow, bringing things up-to-date. In our efforts to ensure that we set the parameters for Rule 68 appropriate -- in an appropriate way for this case, we are considering the requests by the accused Ojdanic, as he sent a detailed request setting his parameters, and we are considering those. It is rather helpful to have those parameters in mind because of the proximity of the two accused, in association with the two accused. I'll hand it over to Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have something to say with respect to procedure. One more technical matter, if I may. I was informed yesterday that for this week, we have a new witness, Merovci, who would be heard immediately after the secret witness that nobody has ever heard of. So once again, I demand that the order of witnesses be ascertained for at least one week and not to have changes and surprises each week which I cannot hear about when I'm in the detention centre during the weekend. I hear about them on a Monday, usually by the end of business on Monday, as to who the next witness will be or the witness after. And usually there's somebody new who appears every time whose statement I do not have or whose statement I received the night before and so on and so forth. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us see what the position is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Merovci was originally scheduled as the very first witness in the case so that he should have been the subject of preparation at that stage. He was unable to attend at that early stage and eventually became available whenever it was, I think last week, and he was notified as a witness coming this week last Thursday, so the accused should have had a week to remind himself of the preparation he no doubt would already have made at the beginning of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Clearly, though, it is -- just a moment. Clearly it's difficult for him in the circumstances which he's in in the Detention Unit. So we must ask you to keep this to a minimum. How long will this witness be, the next two witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It will take all of tomorrow, I'm sure. The first witness won't take very long, but once we start K3, that will take all of tomorrow, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes. No. We -- we --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is quite untrue that I was informed on Thursday. The Registrar informed me of this yesterday, just yesterday, on the first working day of the week, that Merovci has been included for testimony this week. I received no information on Thursday. It was the last working day last week and I did not receive any information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will -- we will see in future that you are informed as early as possible. That particular witness will not be giving evidence today or tomorrow but, at the very earliest, on Thursday. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The Prosecution calls Mr. Mr. Isuf Loku. And, Your Honours, while we're waiting for the witness to come in, the evidence of this witness will pertain to an area that is depicted on page 12 of your Kosovo atlas, at the very bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sir, is your name Isuf Loku?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And Mr. Loku, were you born on the 2nd of August in 1965?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were you born in the village of Kotlina in the municipality of Kacanik in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Is the village of Kotlina to the south of the town of Kacanik?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Loku, on the 11th of June, 1999, did you provide a statement to representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor concerning events that you witnessed and experienced earlier in 1999 in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And on the 11th of March this year, 2002, in the village of Kotlina, in the municipality of Kacanik, in the presence -- were you provided with a copy of the statement that you had made in 1999 in the presence of representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor and a presiding officer appointed by the Registrar of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And at that time, were you able to confirm that the copy of the statement provided to you was true and correct?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would offer the statement of Mr. Loku into evidence under Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 144.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, Isuf Loku is a 36-year-old Kosovo Albanian man from the village of Kotlina in the municipality of Kacanik. Mr. Loku lives in the hamlet of Dreshec in Kotlina. Mr. Loku's statement describes how his village was attacked by Serb forces on the 8th or 9th of March, 1999. Mr. Loku hid nearby and observed that shelling was coming from the direction of Globocica. Among the Serb forces were 13 tanks and two armoured personnel carriers. Mr. Loku observed VJ soldiers and policemen entering his village. Mr. Loku observed as these Serb forces looted and burned the homes in his village. Seventeen homes were burned in the village that day. Several days after this attack, Mr. Loku found the bodies of two residents from Kotlina. On the morning of 24 March 1999, Serb forces began to shell Mr. Loku's village again. Mr. Loku and some relatives hid on the Sheshi mountain nearby. Mr. Loku observed Serb forces advancing toward Kotlina. Again, he saw tanks and armoured personnel carriers. Shortly thereafter, Mr. Loku saw flames coming from the centre of Kotlina. Mr. Loku returned to his village at about 8.00 in the evening. He found one of his neighbours, Zymer Loku, who was badly wounded by machine-gun fire and subsequently died. At about 10.00 that same evening, Mr. Loku and other residents of his village decided to flee to Macedonia. Mr. Loku arrived in Macedonia early in the morning of 25 March 1999. Two of Mr. Loku's brothers disappeared after the attack on Kotlina on the 24th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to you, the village of Kotlina, on the 8th or 9th of March, 1999, was attacked by artillery fire; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did that happen; on the 8th or the 9th?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: On the 9th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, again according to you, after that attack, the attack that followed from all sides - that's what you said - but mostly from the direction of Globocica and the village of -- it says here Gurri i Zi, I don't know what we call that in Serbian, and from the local Kashani road, all the inhabitants flew from the village to take to -- fled from the village to take to the mountains, Mount Sheshi; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then that means -- or let me put it in the form of a question. Does that mean that, as you say, the Serbs in fact attacked an empty village if, as you say, all the inhabitants had taken to the Sheshi mountains? So the Serbs in fact attacked an empty village, and they shelled it and fought to gain control, you say, from 7.00 until 11.00 on that same day. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: They shelled it from the -- from 9.00 to 11.00 from Gllobocica village. Then they arrived in our village, looted it and raided it and burned the houses. That was how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you -- and I'm taking this question by question. You said everybody left. They went to hide and then they fought to gain control of the village from 7.00 to 11.00. Now, tell me, please, what stopped the Serb forces for a full four hours from entering the village which, as you say, was empty? So what stopped the Serbs from entering for a period of four hours?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: They shelled the village for three hours, and then after that, they arrived in our village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The question, I think, was this: Was there any reason you could see why they couldn't go into the village earlier? Was there any reason that occurred to you why that couldn't be done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First they shelled it from Gllobocica. After the shelling stopped, they came to the village, they arrived in our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how far away is Mount Sheshi from your village?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: It is very close to the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I guess it is close if you fled to the Sheshi mountains. But I'm just asking you how nearby or how far away it is.

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: It is about 50 metres away from my own house, where we had taken shelter in that mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh. You fled into a mountain that was 50 metres away from the village?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: We left our houses after the shelling, and we stayed there, close by, as I said. Only after the shelling we left the houses and took refuge in the Sheshi mountain, where we stayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. When you sought shelter there, when you fled from your houses, if I understand you correctly, you found shelter 50 metres away from your house. So you fled only 50 metres away from your house. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: My brothers and my neighbours were there. The others went in the direction of the centre of the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Loku, it was the distance which we're concerned about. The translation appears to have come out as the mountains being 50 metres from your house. Is that right, 50 metres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's be very specific about this. Mount Sheshi is 50 metres away from your house; right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. It is about 50 metres. But the mountains is quite high, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: After the shelling, you fled 50 metres away from your house and you felt safe there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: It was not that we felt safe there, but that was the only place we could go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. When the Serb forces entered the village, did they do anything to you, because you stayed there 50 metres away from house, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: They didn't see us. They entered the houses, they raided them, they looted them, then burned them, and then left later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you were 50 metres away from your house, but they did not see you; right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How did you manage to hide that way? Where is it that you were hiding?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: It is a mountain with forests, and we hid there and stayed there all day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how many of you were there there?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Thirteen people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thirteen of you were 50 metres away from the house and nobody saw you?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Loku, perhaps you can help us with this concept of 50 metres. If you look at this courtroom, from that end to that end, how would you say the distance was that you fled in relation to the distance in this courtroom? Was it twice as long, thrice as long or six times as long, or how would you put it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was three times as big.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Three times as long.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As long, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Than you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Actually, I don't know whether it's worth continuing, but I shall continue my questions. Who did you see? You were watching the soldiers enter the village. They were 50 metres away from you. Who did you see?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: We saw Serb and police -- Serb army and police. They were the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. ones that we saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: There were many. I couldn't count them. They were together, army and police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Approximately, what does "many" mean? Was there a thousand of them, 2.000, 5.000, 500? How many of them were there, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: I saw about 25 near my own house. That was the closest possible distance I could see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Near your house. And you didn't see anybody else but those 25 soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you see anybody else apart from these 25 soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: No. I saw only those soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So according to what you have been claiming, it is 25 soldiers that entered your village. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. To be fair to the witness, he didn't say that. He said he saw 25.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely what I'm asking him. He is testifying about the number of soldiers that entered the village. He said that he saw 25 of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. That's as far as he can say. He saw 25 himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many of them were policemen and how many were soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: I think about ten were policemen and the others were soldiers. I'm talking about those who were near my own house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, how did they arrive there? Did they come in some kind of vehicles or did they come on foot?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: They came there by tanks, armoured cars, trucks; all sorts of vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many tanks did you see?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Thirteen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how many armoured vehicles did you see?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: I saw two armoured vehicles. There may be more, but I only saw two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And how many trucks did you see?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Ten trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In 13 tanks, ten trucks, and two armoured vehicles, that's a total of 25 combat and non-combat vehicles, that is to say combat and transport vehicles. Those are the ones you saw with your own eyes. Twenty-five soldiers and policemen arrived in these vehicles. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is not fair. What he said was that he saw 25 near his house. He's also said that there were a large number of vehicles, which he's described. Now, that's his evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not that way, Mr. May. If you look at the transcript, you will see what I asked him. I asked him whether the soldiers and the policemen came on foot or in vehicles. His answer was that they came on tanks, in armoured vehicles, and trucks. And I asked him how these 25 soldiers came to his place, and that was his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have a picture of a large force arriving in trucks to the village, and 25 being seen, 25 soldiers and police being seen by the witness. Perhaps we should ask him this question: Do you know if any police or soldiers went to any other houses besides your house?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just let the witness answer. Let the witness answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand that you were asking him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, they did, they went to other houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Tell us what happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could see them looting, raiding the houses, and burning them afterwards. This is what happened.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I proceed now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A short while ago, you said that you saw these 25 soldiers around your own house. Now you're saying that you saw soldiers around other houses as well. How many soldiers and policemen did you see around other houses?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: I don't know around the other houses. They were further away. I saw them, but I don't know how many there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. A minute ago you said that they were going to other houses, that you saw them going to other houses, and now you say you don't know what happened, that they were further away. Now, which one is the truth; what you said a minute ago or what you're saying now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You know, you must be fair to the witness. There's not necessarily a distinction. He saw soldiers going to other houses, but he doesn't know how many.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, we hear what his answers are. There is no need for you to interpret his answers. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. There's no reason for you to be unfair to the witness and put to him things which he didn't say. But let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, now, in your village were there ever any members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes, there were -- there were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The interpretation I got was yes, there were, and then there were not. Now, just tell me yes or no. Were there any or were there not any?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: No, there were not. There were no KLA in Kotlina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And then, in your opinion, why were the Serbs shelling an empty village, and why did they manage to enter this empty village only four hours after they had started shelling? Empty village from 7.00 to 11.00, they are shelling an empty village, and then they entered at 11.00 and there's no one in there. Why?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a matter for them. You'll have to ask the Serb forces that. It's not for him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That seems logical to you, Mr. May; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness can't answer for somebody else. If you've got a comment about his evidence, you can make it in due course. Now, let's get on to the next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 1 of your statement, in the fourth paragraph, you say -- you can take a look at it now. The Serbs entered your village with 13 tanks, trucks, two combat vehicles, and there were -- there were several thousand Serb soldiers. That's what you say. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, now, could you please explain this to me? I asked you how many entered, and you explained to me that there were 25, that you saw 25 and that you didn't see anybody else, and in the statement you wrote that there were several thousand of them. And I will remind you that I asked you, when you said "many," I said, "How many? 500, 1.000, 2.000, 5.000?" And then in response to that, you said 25. And in the statement, it says several thousand. Now you said 25. Could you please explain this?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: There were those that I saw near my house, but those that I didn't see around the other houses. There were a lot more around other houses but I saw these 25 were around my house. The others I don't know, but there were a lot more of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I asked you, apart from those whom you saw near your house, how many soldiers and policemen were in the village, and you said to me that you don't know, that you only saw 25. In the statement that you signed, you wrote that there were several thousand of them. When were you telling the truth; then or now? Tell me.

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Well, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. If that is correct, what could have prevented several thousand soldiers from entering that small village of yours? Why did they have to wait for four hours? What do you think? Several thousand people. Several thousand people entering into Kotlina.

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: I don't know. You may know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But it is certain that you claim that there were several thousand of them; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's move on. You've made that point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how many there were. There were a lot of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know -- please, listen to me carefully and give me an accurate answer to my question. Do you know that it is precisely in your village that one of the well-known prisons was where the KLA held detained Albanians who were loyal to the authorities? Yes or no. Please give me an answer. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: There was no prison there. This isn't true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that this same kind of prison existed in the village of Ivaja?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: There wasn't. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how far away is the village of Ivaja from your village?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: It's five kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And I assume that you know this village well.

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Can you tell me how many members of the KLA were in the school, clinic, and mosque in your village on that day?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not from Ivaja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I said your village. In the following buildings: The school, the clinic and the mosque of your village.

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's being suggested, Mr. Loku, that on the day of the attack, the 8th of March, that there were KLA members in the school, clinic, and the mosque. Now, is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, Milaim Loku, was he related to you?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: He's a distant cousin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that he was the commander of this so-called sub-command of the 162nd Brigade of the KLA, the so-called Kacanik Brigade, and it was precisely for the village of Kotlina? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: No, he wasn't a commander. He wasn't a soldier. He was a civilian. There was no KLA in Kotlina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You claim that he and Emerllah Kuci were killed by sniper fire. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes, on the 9th of March. He was killed after a river [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that your relative Milaim Loku lost his life precisely in that capacity, as commander of this sub-staff of the 162nd Brigade of the KLA in their clash with the army and the police?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: He was killed by Serbian forces. He was a civilian. Milaim Loku, and Emerllah Kuci, both of them were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, where were they when they were killed?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: They were in the village, near the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that means that they were in your village, in the village of Kotlina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How could they be there when, in response to the first question I put to you, you answered that all the inhabitants of the village had left Kotlina?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: I saw them on the 10th of March, after the Serbian forces left. That's when I found them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you said that all the inhabitants of the village had left Kotlina. Why did they stay on there?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: They didn't go away. They hid. They were in Kotlina, in the village. Everybody was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's time for the adjournment now. We'll adjourn for 20 minutes. Mr. Loku, could you remember in this adjournment not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and not to let anybody speak to you about it, including the members of the Prosecution team. Could you be back, please, in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that there were no KLA members in your village and that the relatives of yours --

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- are not members of the KLA. Tell me this now: Where were the closest KLA members in terms of your village? If they weren't in your village actually, where were they? What was the closest point at which they were to your village?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: There was no KLA in Kotlina. I repeat it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about Kotlina now. What I'm asking you is near Kotlina, how far off were they? Not in Kotlina. You said they were not in Kotlina. All right, then, but how far off were they? Where were they if they weren't in Kotlina?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: The KLA was a long way away, in the village of Ivaja. There was KLA there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that the village of Ivaja was five kilometres away from your own village; right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, the soldiers whom you say entered your village, the several thousands of soldiers, as you said, first passed through Ivaja or did they first go through your own village?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: On the previous day, they had been Ivaja, but they came -- on the 8th they were in Ivaja, on the 9th they came to Kotlina but they didn't come through Ivaja, they came through Gllobocica and Gurri i Zi.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And how long did the fighting go on for in Ivaja?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: All day. All day. I don't know; I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All day. What does that mean? From morning to night or what? Or did it go on after dark as well?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: From morning to midday probably. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how many KLA forces were in Ivaja?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since the fighting went on from morning to noon, to the afternoon, I assume that there were quite a lot of KLA members in Ivaja. Did they escape? Did they flee from Ivaja in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how do you know then that the fighting went on from morning to afternoon?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Because I heard the gunfire from morning to noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, afterwards, after this clash had ended, that is to say between the army and the KLA in Ivaja, did you meet members of the KLA? Did you come across them, you and the inhabitants of your village?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: I didn't meet them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Not even afterwards, over the next few days? You didn't meet them then either?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: I didn't meet them ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is Hazbi Loku a relative of yours too?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: He is a distant relative. He is a cousin but a distant one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, was he a member of the KLA units?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since he's a distant relative, is that something that you know for sure or do you only assume that to be true?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: No. I know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that Hazbi Loku is a witness here in The Hague as well?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did you see him last?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Two months ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you talk about your testimony here and his testimony?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So both you and he know that you're going to testify in The Hague, but you didn't discuss it amongst yourselves; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me this: From your family, both distant family and close relatives, how many of them were members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: There were no members of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, is it true, in connection with the event that you describe, that already on the next day, that is to say after the alleged attack by the Serb forces on your village in Kotlina, that the OSCE appeared?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes, on the 10th of March. That was when the OSCE came.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Three.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Three individuals. So just one OSCE vehicle; is that right? Just one vehicle arrived?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: First came one. Then came others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean when you say one and then another. You mean one vehicle and then another vehicle? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: I meant that, later, five others came.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's clear this up. So three men arrived in one vehicle first and then five others, five other people in the second vehicle. So this makes eight people in two vehicles; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: In Dreshec neighbourhood came only one. Four others came in the centre of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't follow you. What do you mean when you say in the village of Dreshec? Your village is named Kotlina. Did they come to Kotlina or did they come to Dreshec?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Dreshec is a neighbourhood. I said a neighbourhood. I didn't say a village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But I assume that they made a tour of the whole village.

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did anyone, any of the authorities - Serbia, Kosovo, Yugoslavia - was any official together with them or were they alone?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: This I don't know. I have no information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But you saw them. You say you saw them and that there were three plus five, which makes a total of eight. Did anybody else come with them?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: There was the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how long did they stay in your village?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: They stayed there the whole day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did they give you any kind of assistance on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: They took the inhabitants of Dreshec neighbourhood to Kacanik. Only the inhabitants of Dreshec neighbourhood because the houses were burned. Women, children, and elderly people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how many houses are there in that part of town, the part of town that is called Dreshec, the Dreshec neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Seventeen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that in the other part of the village, that is to say in the village proper, that the houses were all right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: That day, they only raided and looted those villages in the centre of the -- the houses in the village, in the centre of the village, on the 9th of March. They didn't burn them that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you said that the village was shelled for several hours. How come then that the houses weren't destroyed if the village had indeed been shelled for several hours?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: The infantry troops came and set fire to the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Dreshec neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In the Dreshec neighbourhood. You said that it comprised 17 houses, and Kotlina itself was not damaged. Is that what you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. said? Did I understand you to say that?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. Only -- they only raided the houses in the centre of the village on the 9th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That's why I'm asking you. How is it possible that Kotlina remained untouched, was not damaged, if it had been shelled for a period of several hours, as you yourself described, before the forces actually entered the village?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: The whole village was burned on the 24th of March, afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you help us as to this: The point that's made is if there was shelling, were the houses damaged by the shelling or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some were damaged, some not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did the representatives of the OSCE give you any kind of assistance? Did they help you in any way, apart from taking the inhabitants of that part of the village which is called Dreshec away to Kacanik, as you yourself said?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: They brought some assistance to the sick people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there a doctor among them perhaps?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the people they helped, what were they suffering from? Why did they need help?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: I don't know. They were sick.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And Naim Loku and Lulezim Loku, were they also members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: No, they were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: According to you, during the second attack launched on Kotlina, which took place, once again according to your own explanation, on the 24th of March, 1999, you say you watched the attack and saw the arrival, as you say, of the Serb forces from a distance of about two kilometres. So you watched all this from a distance of about two kilometres. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was that not the same position that you were in when you watched the attack on the 8th and the 9th?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: No. It was elsewhere. I was near the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When were you near the centre?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: On the 24th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you say that you watched the attack take place from a distance of approximately two kilometres.

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: I was closer than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, let's clear this up. You say that you were close to the centre, near the centre, and then you also say in your statement that you watched from a distance of two kilometres. So which is correct; that you were near the centre or that you watched from a distance of two kilometres?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: The centre of the village is about two kilometres away from Dreshec neighbourhood, and I was near the centre, I said. And this is from where I saw the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So on the 24th of March, you watched the attack on Dreshec; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: I heard the shells, I saw the shells coming from Gllobocica. Then they arrived in the centre of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you say you were in the centre of the village.

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: I was nearby, close to the centre, not in the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please. You've just explained to us that from close to the centre, from near to the centre with respect to Dreshec, you were two kilometres away. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that the attack was launched on Dreshec. Now, as you say, you were watching the attack from a distance of two kilometres. So the attack was on Dreshec. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. They fired in the direction of Dreshec.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That means that you saw them shooting in the direction of Dreshec on the 24th of March from a distance of two kilometres, which is where you were near the centre of the village. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But a moment ago, you explained that Dreshec had been completely destroyed. That means all 17 houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We go round and round these points. I don't think we're going to get much further with them. The witness has explained the best he can. Now, unless you've got a new point, let's move on rather than spending a lot of time on these distances and descriptions. We'll have to make up our mind about this evidence in due course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but you can't make up your minds unless you hear my questions and his answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Not if there's a vast amount of repetition. Now, you've got about six minutes more of this examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Very well. Let me hurry up then. But the witness is explaining that he watched the attack on Dreshec, which he claims was destroyed on the 9th of March, and that from the centre of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, on the 24th of March, did you happen to see any army or police when this second attack took place?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And where were you watching them from, from that same place near the centre of the village?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: When they came, they came from Gurri i Zi in the direction of Gllobocica, towards the centre. And this is where they stayed. And they killed and looted and burned the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Are you talking about the 24th now or are you going back to the 9th of March? Because you said that they came from Globocica then too.

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: I'm talking about the 24th. They came again from Gllobocica and from Gurri i Zi, but now I'm talking about the 24th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that in the village, at that time when you returned after the attack, that you noticed Zymer Loku who was wounded, who had been wounded; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where was he wounded?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: He was wounded in the right hand and in the right arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you what place he was at when he was wounded. So your answer -- according to your answer, he was in the village. You found him in the village. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: He was in his -- near his house. He was injured near the centre. I saw him myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And as you saw him, did you talk to him?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know why he hadn't left the village previously then, like the rest of the people?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: All were there. He was injured. He couldn't go to Kacanik. The others were killed and massacred and taken to Kacanik. He told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the 24th of March, in your village, were there any KLA members?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: No, there weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you're claiming that nobody in your village lost their lives in the fighting between them and the forces of Yugoslavia and Serbia.

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: The Serbs captured them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who did they capture?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Twenty-two were massacred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that they captured them.

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What happened next, after they had captured them?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: They massacred, they buried them in a hole and covered the hole.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: I didn't see that when it happened, but after they left, I went to that site.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what did you see at that site?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: They had covered them with earth. I saw some clothes lying around, some boots, some shoes. That was all I saw. It was night also.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how did you know they had been massacred if they'd already been buried?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Zymer Loku told me. He was injured but still alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but that means that everything you're saying now is things that in fact you heard from others. You saw none of that yourself; right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: I saw Zymer Loku myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You saw Zymer Loku who was wounded. Yes. You saw him. But all the rest of it, everything else you've been talking about is something that you heard from him or from others. You didn't actually see it yourself; right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I was close by, but I didn't see it with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, have you got any questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before this is continued, since you've provided a lot of these documents, as regards this book and its admission into evidence, I did not ask for the entire book to be admitted. I just asked for one sentence of Robert Gelbard to be admitted, and that has to do with defining the KLA as a terrorist organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will consider that in a moment, but let's finish with this witness first.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought that this witness was finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Loku, how many hamlets or neighbourhoods make up the village of Kotlina?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Three neighbourhoods.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So besides Dreshec, what are the other two neighbourhoods of Kotlina?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Reka and Dreshec. Dreshec and Reka and the centre of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And are those three hamlets spread around the base of a mountain that you refer to as the Sheshi mountain?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Let's talk for a moment regarding the 9th of March, when your village was attacked. When the shelling began, were you at home?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were your neighbours also at home?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when people began to flee into the forest nearby, and you say you hid with a total of 13 people in one spot, had those persons all been at home when the shelling began?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. They all had been at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Have you done your military service, Mr. Loku?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So you're familiar with firearms and the sounds of firing?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: From the spot where you were hiding on the morning of the 9th of March, did you see or hear any return fire coming from your neighbourhood, Dreshec, going against the Serb forces who were entering?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: From the spot where you were hiding, did you see or hear return fire against the Serb forces coming from anywhere?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned that you saw policemen and soldiers close to your house. Can you briefly describe the uniforms worn by the policemen that you saw?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. It was blue, blue. The police were wearing blue uniform; the army, green uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: On the police uniforms, did you notice -- were you close enough to notice any writing on the blue uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. On their left arm they, had the insignia "Milicija."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Let's move briefly to the 24th of March. Can you explain where you were hiding on the Sheshi mountain that day?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: It was in a high place but near the centre of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could you actually see the centre of the village from where you were hiding on the 24th of March?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: I didn't see it with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: On the 24th of March, did you see or hear any return fire being directed against the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned, on the 24th of March that "they arrived in the centre of the village." Who do you mean by "they"?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: The Serb police and army troops. Those are what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: After the Serb forces arrived in the centre of the village, what, if anything, could you see coming from the centre of the village?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: After they left, I went and saw that the houses of the village were burned. The house -- the school was burned, the out-patient clinic was burned, the mosque was damaged but not burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Whilst the Serb forces were in the centre of Kotlina on the 24th of March, were you able to see any flames coming from the centre of the village?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. I saw the flames and the smoke rising up in the sky.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Later that evening, you mentioned that you spoke to a wounded man named Zymer Loku, and in the translation it came through on the English transcript that Mr. Zymer Loku had been wounded in the arm and the hand. Did you say the arm and the hand or the leg and the hand?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: In the leg and in the arm. In both places. In the right arm and leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did Mr. Loku subsequently die from his wounds?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes, after two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What did Mr. Loku tell you about the fate of the 22 men who had been captured in Kotlina that day?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: He said to me that the Serb forces came and captured them. They took women -- some of the women and children to Kacanik, some they massacred. He said, "I was injured, and I could see it."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did Mr. Loku tell you how the men were massacred?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: He had seen them from a distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What did he say, if anything, about how the men were massacred?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: He said that they took them from that ambulance building and took them to a higher place. They beat them and then they massacred them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned in your cross-examination that these 22 men who were massacred had been buried in a hole. Did you mean a hole or a well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm trying to clarify what might be a translation error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, but it's a very leading question, Mr. Saxon, and on rather an important issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What sort of a hole was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a hole dug by a villager to look for water, but he didn't find water and the hole was still open. That was it. Like a well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Before the attack on the 24th of March, had that hole or well been -- was it still open?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes, it was still open.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: During the attack on the 24th of March, did you hear any explosions that day?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes. I heard two explosions. It was about 5.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when you came back to your village subsequently, what condition was that hole or well in?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: It was covered with earth. It was flattened out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Have those 22 men been seen alive since that day, the 24th of March?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Loku, you told about the massacre of 22 young men who were buried in the hole. You told us that you heard that incident from Mr. Zymer Loku. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How did Mr. Zymer Loku know about the incident? Was he one of the captured men or --

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: He was there, and he had seen when they took them, those 22 people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How did he -- I'm not clear. Did you say that he was one of the captured men? Yes or no? Let me check it.

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: He was injured. He was not captured. He only saw the others being captured and taken up to that place where the hole was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where did he see the incident?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: He was near his own house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You said you know Mr. Hazbi Loku, who is a distant cousin of yours.

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, where does he live? Does he live nearby from you?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: No. He lives in the neighbourhood of Reka, the other neighbourhood that's called Reka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Milaim Loku is a brother of his?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you hear about the massacre of 22 young men from Mr. Hazbi Loku?

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you heard about that incident from two men; Mr. Zymer Loku and Hazbi Loku.

utterances.speaker: ISUF LOKU
utterances.text: From Zymer Loku.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not from Hazbi Loku?
